title: Air India Express and the aviation worker
author: Editorial Desk
summary: In December 2025 BMS asked the Civil Aviation Ministry to examine a crisis at Air India Express.
body:
*Photo: BMS statement on Air India Express, December 2025*

In December 2025, Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS) issued a press statement on what it called a labour crisis at Air India Express, and asked the Ministry of Civil Aviation to step in. The statement is dated 9 December 2025 and was published on the BMS website the following day. It drew a comparison with the disruption at IndiGo that had been in the news, and it reminded readers that Air India Express had faced a similar episode in May 2024. This post explains what BMS said, what happened in 2024, what the record shows, and why a trade union speaks about an airline at all.

One note on method. The claims about the present working conditions at the airline are allegations made by BMS in its own statement. The airline's response is not part of that statement, so they should be read as the union's position and not as findings of fact. The events of May 2024, on the other hand, were widely reported and are described below from news reports.

## What the BMS statement says

According to the BMS press note, the airline is facing a crisis of the kind seen at IndiGo, and the earlier crisis of 7 to 9 May 2024 at Air India Express went largely unnoticed because the country was in the middle of Parliamentary elections. BMS lists a number of complaints on behalf of cabin crew: mental harassment, discrimination and victimisation of members of the Cabin Crew Union, inadequate rest, a rostering system the union calls illogical, and a human-resources approach it describes as authoritarian. It also says the airline has lengthened working hours and reduced the rest between flights, and that management treats the practices of other carriers as a market trend to be copied.

BMS adds that, in its view, management does not give due respect to the union, to senior officials of the Labour Ministry or to the aviation regulator, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA). Its demand is specific. The Ministry of Civil Aviation should intervene immediately and hold talks with the Air India Express Employees' Union so that further unrest is avoided.

## What happened in May 2024

The episode BMS refers to is well documented. In the first week of May 2024, a large section of Air India Express cabin crew reported sick at short notice. Reports at the time said that cancellations began on the night of 7 May and ran through 8 May and beyond. Different reports gave different counts of cancelled flights, from about 74 in the airline's own early figure to more than 80 and nearly 90 in other reports, which is a reminder that numbers in a fast-moving story differ by source and by hour. The airline, which at the time was running about 380 services a day, cancelled flights across many airports, including Delhi, Bengaluru and all four airports in Kerala. One report put the number of stranded passengers at nearly 15,000 over the disruption.

The airline's first response was severe. It described the absences as a concerted abstention from work without justification and terminated about 25 senior cabin crew members, with some reports saying about 30. Terminated staff lost access to company systems and to benefits for themselves and their dependants. The airline offered passengers on cancelled flights a full refund or free rescheduling.

The Ministry of Civil Aviation asked the airline for a report on the cancellations and asked it to resolve the issues with its staff promptly and to see that passengers were looked after as per DGCA norms. The way out came through conciliation. Meetings led by the Chief Labour Commissioner in New Delhi, attended by the airline and the Air India Express Employees' Union, ended with the crew withdrawing their action and the airline withdrawing the termination letters. All the crew who had reported sick were reported to have rejoined duty by 11 May, and the airline said the network would be stabilised within days. Air India supported the airline on some routes during the crisis.

The union said at that time that the crew's grievances were about alleged mismanagement. It also raised a practical problem: a scheduling-software glitch had left some crew who were back on duty still marked as on sick leave, and re-rostering took time because of medical checks and the need to rebuild duty rosters.

## Why a union speaks about an airline

It is fair to ask why a labour federation comments on aviation. The answer is that in aviation, working conditions are not a private matter between employer and employee. Crew rest, duty hours and rosters are tied to safety rules, and a roster that is built without enough buffer makes delays more likely. When many people are scheduled tightly and one disruption occurs, the failure spreads across the whole network and lands on passengers who have nothing to do with the dispute.

For that reason, an airline is a good example of a point that BMS makes in many sectors: when a service fails repeatedly, one should look at working conditions as well as management decisions. A crew member who is tired, who feels unheard, or who fears punishment for raising a concern is not in the best position to run a safe and punctual operation.

## The numbers and dates to keep in mind

- 7 to 9 May 2024: the cabin crew disruption at Air India Express, as described in the BMS statement and in news reports.
- 8 May 2024: the Civil Aviation Ministry sought a report from the airline.
- About 25 crew were terminated and then reinstated after conciliation led by the Chief Labour Commissioner.
- About 380 daily services was the size of the airline's operation at the time.
- 9 December 2025: the date of the BMS statement calling for intervention.

## What BMS is asking, in plain terms

Stripped of the detail, the BMS ask has three parts. First, that the Ministry of Civil Aviation treat the matter as a policy question and not only as a company matter. Second, that the airline sit down with the recognised employee union and talk before a dispute turns into cancelled flights. Third, that duty-time and rest rules be followed in practice and not only on paper. None of these demands requires anyone to take a side in a commercial contest. They are the kind of steps that normally precede a settlement.

## What remains to be done

Several questions are still open, and a reader should keep them in mind. Is there enough crew and ground staff for the number of flights? Are the rest rules being followed, and who checks? What is the regulator's role when disruptions repeat? How are crew grievances heard before they become a crisis? The BMS statement raises these questions but does not answer them, and the answers would have to come from the airline, the DGCA and the Ministry. A fair reading is that a regular, structured dialogue between management and the union is the cheapest safeguard against a repeat of May 2024.

## A practical point for travellers

For people who fly, the lesson is practical. Behind every delayed flight there is a system of people who work to a schedule, and when the system is strained the traveller feels it first. Passengers have rights to refunds or rescheduling when flights are cancelled, as the airline itself offered in 2024, but a more reliable service depends on workers who are rested, respected and heard. The BMS statement is a reminder that labour relations and public service are connected, and that a workplace which is respected is more likely to be a workplace that functions.
